title: The Moral Foundations of Politics
coreMove: Translate a political claim into the moral foundations it is activating before deciding what it means.
sourcePressure: The chapter applies multiple moral foundations to political life and treats disagreement as different moral emphases.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer makes political rivals defective rather than differently tuned across foundations.

sourceAnchors.name: moral foundations
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar identifies moral foundations as the bridge from moral psychology into politics.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A political slogan can be decoded by asking which foundation it is asking to wake up.

sourceAnchors.name: political disagreement
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar says disagreement often reflects different moral emphases rather than a total absence of concern.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The other side may be protecting a different moral load-bearing wall, not simply ignoring the house.

hook: Do not open ch07 with a person discovering that morality is complicated.
Do not use 'you think X, but actually Y' as the hook shell.
counterintuition: Avoid treating the opposing view as stupid before explaining the mechanism.
tryThisNow: No generic write down your values prompt.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.audience: civic organizers hearing rival moral languages
exampleSpecs.stakes: Anna decodes each slogan by foundation before rewriting the flyer.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Anna places commuter safety, taxpayer fairness, and neighborhood loyalty on separate sticky notes.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A transit map covers the folding table from edge to edge.

exampleSpecs.domain: immigration clinic preparing clients for a hostile council meeting
exampleSpecs.audience: advocates translating claims across moral frames
exampleSpecs.stakes: Javier reframes the appeal so authority and loyalty concerns are acknowledged before contested.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Javier rehearses a sentence that names residents' order concern before defending the clinic.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Say the word order before they accuse you of ignoring it," Javier tells the volunteer.

exampleSpecs.domain: rural broadband coalition uniting farmers and remote workers
exampleSpecs.stakes: Min identifies which foundation each subgroup needs the project to satisfy.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Min rewrites the pitch so one page speaks fairness and another speaks loyalty to town survival.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Dust from the grain elevator settles on the laptops after the community meeting.

exampleSpecs.domain: parent group fighting over school phone rules
exampleSpecs.stakes: Margaux shows that one side hears protection and the other hears autonomy.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Margaux split the comments into care, authority, and fairness before proposing a trial.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You see confiscated phones lined up in numbered envelopes.

exampleSpecs.domain: environmental lawsuit communication team choosing public language
exampleSpecs.audience: lawyers explaining a case beyond legal terms
exampleSpecs.stakes: David translates the same river case through harm, loyalty, and sanctity without changing facts.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 9:30, David asks which version each audience will call moral common sense before revealing the split.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 9:30, David writes the river's name three times on the glass wall.

exampleSpecs.domain: hospital allocation committee after a scarce-bed decision
exampleSpecs.audience: ethics committee members managing public explanation
exampleSpecs.stakes: Marit separates fairness outrage from care outrage in family complaints.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Marit tags each complaint by moral emphasis before drafting the apology.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Marit one night of voicemails to hear two kinds of pain in the same accusation.

skillTargets: decode a political claim into foundation language
avoid assuming absence of morality in the opposing side
separate diagnosis of moral emphasis from policy endorsement

tryThisNowSpec: Translate one political sentence into the foundation it protects, then write a reply that names that concern before disagreeing.
